summary:
This work identifies hydrogen tunneling as a plausible microscopic origin of two-level systems (TLS) in native Nb$_2$O$_5$ and Ta$_2$O$_5$ oxides that limit superconducting-qubit coherence and SRF-cavity quality factors. Machine-learned interatomic potentials accelerate sampling of hydrogen configurations and diffusion barriers in amorphous oxides, revealing that H is the only light interstitial with barrier–distance combinations yielding tunnel splittings in the $

motivation: TLS in Nb and Ta pentoxides are a bottleneck for qubit coherence times and cavity $Q$ factors, yet their microscopic origin remains unknown despite clear experimental trends: higher loss in Nb than Ta (30% difference), correlation with oxygen vacancies and amorphous disorder, and stronger H incorporation in Nb oxide.
method: The authors sampled $\sim$10,000 relaxed hydrogen interstitial sites in each 49-structure ensemble of amorphous Nb$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$ and Ta$_2$O$_{5-\delta}$ (49 cells per oxide, 162–168 atoms each, seven oxygen-vacancy levels) using MLIP-accelerated NEB to map diffusion barriers, then computed tunnel splittings $\Delta$ via quartic WKB approximation and extracted TLS statistics to estimate effective TLS densities and dielectric loss.
result: At hydrogen concentrations of $\sim$2 at.% in Nb$_2$O$_5$ and $\sim$1 at.% in Ta$_2$O$_5$, the model predicts $\tan\delta_0 \approx 8.6 \times 10^{-4}$ and $6.7 \times 10^{-4}$ respectively, consistent with measured loss of $(8.1{-}18) \times 10^{-4}$ for Nb and the observed $\sim$30% lower loss in Ta oxide, with the difference arising from atomistically derived pair statistics showing higher probability of microwave-active H tunneling in Nb.
